Who Holds the Power?.e: An enumerated national power. States are expressly forbidden to coin money.
A reserved power under the Tenth Amendment.
Forbidden to both levels by Article I.

Who Holds the Power?.q: Set rules for marriage and divorce
Who Holds the Power?.e: Reserved to the states, within constitutional limits.
The president makes treaties with the Senate’s consent. States are forbidden to.

Who Holds the Power?.q: Run elections, including for federal offices
Who Holds the Power?.e: States administer elections within rules set by the Constitution and Congress.
Forbidden to both Congress and the states.
Congress creates lower federal courts; every state has its own courts.

Who Holds the Power?.q: Regulate commerce within a single state
Who Holds the Power?.e: Intrastate commerce is reserved to the states — though the Court lets Congress reach local activity with a substantial effect on interstate commerce.

Who Holds the Power?.q: Set rules for naturalizing new citizens
Who Holds the Power?.e: Naturalization is an enumerated power of Congress.

Who Holds the Power?.q: Tax goods exported from a state
Who Holds the Power?.e: Congress may not tax exports; states may not tax imports or exports without Congress’s consent.

Who Holds the Power?.q: Create local governments such as cities and counties
Who Holds the Power?.e: Local governments are creations of their states.
Each level makes and enforces laws within its own sphere.
The Commerce Clause gives this to Congress.
Forbidden to both Congress and the states.

Grants and Mandates.q: Federal money restricted to a specific, narrow purpose
Grants and Mandates.e: The most commonly used form of federal aid; preferred by the national government.

Grants and Mandates.q: Federal money for a broad policy area with minimal restrictions
Grants and Mandates.e: Preferred by states because of its flexibility.

Grants and Mandates.q: Federal money with almost no restrictions on its use
Grants and Mandates.e: The least used form; ran from 1972 to 1986.

Grants and Mandates.q: A requirement the national government places on the states
Grants and Mandates.e: States must comply whether or not money comes with it.

Grants and Mandates.q: Which form of federal funding is most commonly used?
Grants and Mandates.e: Categorical grants make up most federal aid to states.

Grants and Mandates.q: Which form of federal funding do states prefer?
Grants and Mandates.e: Block grants — flexibility. (States liked revenue sharing too, but it is rarely used.)

Grants and Mandates.q: A federal requirement that comes with little or no money to pay for it
Grants and Mandates.e: The Americans with Disabilities Act is a common example.

Grants and Mandates.q: Withholding highway money from states that won’t raise the drinking age to 21
Grants and Mandates.e: Money in one program used to change policy in another area.

Grants and Mandates.q: A condition, such as nondiscrimination, that applies to nearly all federal grants
Grants and Mandates.e: It cuts across programs instead of applying to one.

Grants and Mandates.q: Federal law displacing state law on the same subject
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
o: Made unfunded mandates harder to pass
Grants and Mandates.e: Cost estimates and a floor challenge — not a ban.

Grants and Mandates.q: A program guaranteeing benefits to everyone who meets its eligibility rules
Grants and Mandates.e: Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid are examples.

Clauses and Amendments.e: Also called the elastic clause. Article I.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Makes the Constitution and valid federal laws the supreme law of the land
Clauses and Amendments.e: Article VI. The basis of preemption.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Reserves powers not delegated to the national government to the states or the people
Clauses and Amendments.e: The constitutional home of reserved powers.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Gives Congress power over trade “among the several States”
Clauses and Amendments.e: Article I. At issue in Lopez.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Requires states to honor each other’s public acts, records, and court judgments
Clauses and Amendments.e: Article IV. Governs relations among the states.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Says no state may deny any person due process or equal protection of the laws
Clauses and Amendments.e: Ratified 1868. Shifted power toward the national government.
1913. The money behind modern federal grants.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Moved the election of senators from state legislatures to voters
Clauses and Amendments.e: 1913. State legislatures lost their direct voice in Congress.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Which clause did McCulloch v. Maryland rely on to uphold the national bank?
Clauses and Amendments.e: Implied powers — the bank was a means of carrying out enumerated powers.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Which clause kept Maryland from taxing the national bank?
Clauses and Amendments.e: A state can’t burden a valid federal institution.

Clauses and Amendments.q: Which clause did United States v. Lopez turn on?
Clauses and Amendments.e: Not the Second Amendment — Lopez is about the limits of the commerce power.

Clauses and Amendments.q: The process of applying the Bill of Rights to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment
Clauses and Amendments.e: Case by case, beginning in the 1920s. You’ll study it in depth later.

Federalism Over Time.q: The event that most clearly shifted the nation from dual to cooperative federalism
Federalism Over Time.e: The national response to the Great Depression in the 1930s.

Federalism Over Time.q: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) moved power toward
Federalism Over Time.e: New national limits on what states may do to individuals.

Federalism Over Time.q: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) moved power toward
Federalism Over Time.e: State legislatures no longer chose senators.
Block grants, fewer unfunded mandates, a narrower commerce power.

Federalism Over Time.q: The Welfare Reform Act of 1996 replaced an open-ended program with
Federalism Over Time.e: TANF — a block grant giving states more control. An example of devolution.

Federalism Over Time.q: The Every Student Succeeds Act (2015), replacing No Child Left Behind, gave states
Where the Bill of Rights originally applied
Federalism Over Time.e: Selective incorporation later applied most of it to the states.

Federalism Over Time.q: Which era relied most heavily on revenue sharing?
Federalism Over Time.e: General revenue sharing ran from 1972 to 1986.
